blocks.label: Your four asks, answered

blocks.html:
Ask 1

A plan to rebuild the stage-based flows, prioritised by cohort size

“These predate your work and I don’t think they’ve been touched. Given we know each mom’s stage and sell a consumable, this should be the best-performing thing we own.”

Short answerYes, and I’d start immediately. The problem is bigger than the three flows you named: everything from six months on is earning campaign money on your most personalised asset, and the fix splits into two different jobs.

The curve is steeper than the three you picked: $0.377 a recipient at newborn, $0.0037 at twelve months.

blocks.cap: Nursing and pumping tracks combined, last 90 days.
blocks.title: What each stage earns, against what it sends

blocks.html:
Months zero to five: 219,464 emails a quarter at $0.206 a recipient. Months six to twelve: 239,476 at $0.023. Over half the stage volume goes to mums whose need has largely passed.

Zero to five is a rebuild. The intent is there, the content is old, and this is where your 17,500 new customers from July and August land. Six to twelve is a positioning question, because no rewrite sells lactation support to a mum who has started solids. Worth deciding what we sell that cohort before spending a day on copy.

The order I would work in: months zero to two first, they carry the revenue and the incoming cohort. Then three to five. Then a decision on six to twelve, which may be a shorter track pointed at a different product rather than a rebuild. All of it goes into the same testing cadence as everything else, so each one gets a control and a variant rather than one rewrite and hope.

Ask 2

Your recommendation on campaign cadence

“I’d like to cut volume significantly and reinvest the effort into flows. I’d rather send a quarter as much and have people actually open it.”

Short answerI’d hold the volume and change what we send instead. A cut to a quarter costs about $483.0k a year, and on your own data it would not buy you a better unsubscribe rate: your busiest weeks are already your cleanest.

Sends per week against the unsubscribe rate is -0.54. Busier weeks run a lower rate per recipient, and the five worst weeks of the year were all one and two send weeks. Cadence drives the unsubscribe count (+0.64) only because it drives volume.

The last two quarters ran the test for us. To Jun ’26: 44 campaigns, $138.6k, $0.018 a recipient, 0.191% unsubscribes. To Aug ’26: 60 campaigns, up 36%, $175.4k, up 27%, at $0.023 and 0.183%. More sending, better per recipient, lower rate.

blocks.cap: Last six months. Bars are campaigns sent, the area is campaign revenue, the line is revenue per recipient.
blocks.title: Campaigns sent, what they earned, and what each recipient was worth

blocks.html:
With growth taken out, sends against revenue per campaign is -0.17, so a single campaign earns no less as volume rises.

What I would add rather than subtract is more blog campaigns. In the category report in this tab, blog sends returned the most revenue per send of any category and targeted sends the least, because a targeted send reaches a fraction of the people. Since you are billed per email, revenue per send is the number that decides this, not revenue per recipient.

Happy to stage-target the blog pieces where the subject suits it, but I would not narrow the audience to do it. A piece on sleep regression is still worth reading for a mum whose baby is past it, and worth forwarding to the friend whose baby is not.

On the 15,500 unsubscribes a quarter. You are right that campaigns carry the volume, 67,130 over twelve months against 11,563 from flows. Per email delivered it reverses: 0.60% on flows against 0.23% on campaigns. And no single campaign is doing the damage. Across 81 sends the rate runs 0.108% to 0.294%, median 0.183%, worst one 2.4% of the total.

blocks.cap: 52 weeks, grouped by campaigns per week. Bars are what the week earned, the line is the unsubscribe rate per recipient.
blocks.title: Revenue and unsubscribe rate at each cadence you have run

blocks.cap: Each bar is one campaign. The line is the median at 0.183%.
blocks.title: Every campaign's unsubscribe rate, last 120 days

blocks.html: There is no suppression win left either: campaigns already go to a 90-day engaged segment with seven exclusion lists on top, not the 678,556-profile file. If anything the audience is too tight. About 53,275 people opened or clicked something in the last three to six months but sit outside the 90-day window, so they receive no campaigns at all.

Ask 3

Driving quiz completion, and expanding the subscription flows

“Subs: Upcoming Charge only reached 4,728 people last quarter against ~12,000 orders a month.”

Short answerQuiz: yes, and the cheapest win on this page. Subscriptions: the 4,728 is not the problem it looks like, because that flow can only reach people who are on a subscription, and it is already reaching about 87% of them.

Quiz. $3.54 a recipient, reaching 10,855 people in 90 days, the best numbers in the account. I would put it in the welcome series and post-purchase, and test it as a campaign to the engaged file.

Subscriptions. Loop fired 5,407 upcoming-order events last quarter and the flow delivered to 4,694 of them, so there is no trigger fault to fix. Subscription orders run about 1,127 a month against roughly 10,200 orders in total, one in nine, and last quarter Loop started 2,644 subscriptions and cancelled 2,233, so the base is barely growing. The expansion worth building is the cancel, skip and failed-payment side, plus the push from first order onto subscription, rather than more reach on a flow already reaching nearly everyone eligible.

Ask 4

SMS: worth fixing, or worth switching off?

“188,767 messages last quarter for $1,364 in attributed revenue at a 1.63% unsubscribe rate.”

Short answerHalf off. Your $1.4k is the campaign side and I agree, switch that off until we rebuild it. The SMS flows are a different channel wearing the same name and they earned $18.5k over the same three months. Stop the campaigns, leave the automations running.

blocks.cap: Last three months. The two halves of the channel behave nothing alike.
blocks.title: SMS revenue: flows against campaigns

blocks.html:
One thing you did not ask for

An evergreen best-of flow. Your ten best campaigns of the last 120 days averaged $0.031 a recipient against a $0.022 median at 0.201% unsubscribes. On a flow that content keeps earning, and it gives us something to send those 53,275 warm people outside the campaign audience. It is also the natural place to test the quiz: a best-of flow going to people we do not otherwise reach is a free shot at putting the quiz in front of far more of them.

One heads-up so it does not surprise you later: it will pull the average revenue per recipient across the flows down, because it is campaign content travelling on a flow rail. The revenue it adds is still additional.

What this costs

Nothing extra. The stage rebuild, the quiz work, the subscription flows and the evergreen build all sit inside the current rate. Let’s look at scope again in six months, once the stage tracks are rebuilt and we can see what they are doing.

reports.summary: Your four asks, each with a short answer and the numbers behind it. Three I agree with, one I would change. All of it inside the current retainer.
